unit.label: People & connections
unit.title: A little more to say.
unit.description: 13 new words and forms. More ways to talk about people.

goal.pinyin: tāmen yě shì wǒ de xuéshēng

lessons.title: Talk about other people
lessons.subtitle: He and she, with a familiar pattern

steps.prompt: Which word addresses more than one person: “you” (plural)?
steps.explanation: 你們 (nǐmen) means you when you are speaking to a group.

lessons.title: Say “not”
lessons.subtitle: A small change before the verb

steps.prompt: Someone asks 你是學生嗎？ You are not a student. Which short answer fits?
steps.explanation: 不是 (bú shì) means no, I am not. Repeat 是 in its negative form.
For this meaning, put 也 before 不, then 是: 也不是.

lessons.title: My student, your student
lessons.subtitle: Use 的 to show a connection

steps.prompt: What does 他的學生 mean?
steps.explanation: 他 + 的 + 學生 = his student. 的 links him to the noun; it is not the verb 是.

steps.prompt: Fill the measure-word slot: 一 __ 學生
steps.explanation: 一個學生 = one student. 個 goes between the number and the person you are counting.
一 is yī on its own: one. In 一個, its tone changes to yí.

lessons.title: Have and don’t have
lessons.subtitle: 有, 沒有, and a useful question

steps.prompt: 你有學生嗎？ You do not have any students. Choose the short answer.
steps.explanation: This question uses 有 (have). Its negative answer is 沒有 (do not have). 不是 answers an identity question with 是.
不 goes before 是. 有 is the exception you learned: its negative is 沒有.

newVocabulary.note: An extra everyday form alongside the frequency-list words.
Sounds bú before a fourth tone, as in 不是.
Often light-toned ge in a phrase. Used with 人 and 學生 here.

newVocabulary.meaning: do not have; there is not / are no

他.note: 他 means he or him in this unit. 她 means she or her; both are pronounced tā.
他.memory: Keep the narrow person shape on the left. The three strokes on the right form 也.

parts.label: 亻
parts.name: person
parts.description: The same person component as in 你. It helps connect this character with a person.

parts.label: 也
parts.name: 也 shape
parts.description: 他 and 她 share 也 on the right. The whole characters are pronounced tā; 也 by itself is yě. Do not read this as a modern sound equation.

她.note: 她 is the written pronoun she or her. It sounds exactly like 他 (he or him). The writing and context tell them apart.
她.memory: Reuse 女 from 好, then add the same right side as 他.

parts.label: 女
parts.name: woman
parts.description: 女 is the same component you met in 好. Here it helps distinguish the written pronoun she from 他.

parts.label: 也
parts.name: 也 shape
parts.description: This is the same three-stroke component as in 他. Sharing a component is useful for recognition even when it does not explain the modern pronunciation.

們.note: Add the light-toned 們 to a personal pronoun: 我們 = we, 你們 = you (plural), 他們 = they. It is an ending, not an English-style plural for every noun.
們.memory: A narrow person stands beside a wide door. This is a shape memory aid.

parts.label: 亻
parts.name: person
parts.description: 亻 connects this ending with people. You have already written it in 你 and 他.

parts.label: 門
parts.name: door · mén
parts.description: 門 (mén, door) points toward the sound men. The ending 們 normally has a light neutral tone.

也.note: 也 means also or too. In the sentences here it goes after the person and before 是: 我也是學生 = I am a student too.
也.memory: You have seen this shape inside 他 and 她. Now give it the whole square.

parts.label: 也
parts.name: one whole shape
parts.description: Learn the three-stroke shape as a whole. Its meaning also is not explained by smaller modern pieces.

不.note: 不 goes before 是 to say am not, is not, or are not. Before the fourth tone of 是, bù changes to bú in speech: 不是, bú shì.
不.memory: Start with the horizontal stroke, then place the falling stroke, vertical, and final dot.

parts.label: 不
parts.name: one whole shape
parts.description: The four strokes are most useful as one shape. Their modern forms do not give a reliable meaning story for not.

example.meaning: am not; is not; are not

的.note: 的 links a person to a noun: 我的學生 = my student. In this use, de has a light neutral tone.
的.memory: Find the white-shaped block on the left and the spoon-shaped strokes on the right. Remember the written shapes, not a literal meaning equation.

parts.label: 白
parts.name: 白 · white shape
parts.description: 白 means white on its own. Recognize its five strokes here; white does not explain the possessive use of 的.

parts.label: 勺
parts.name: 勺 · spoon shape
parts.description: The right side is 勺, a three-stroke shape. Learn de with the whole character instead of guessing its sound from this part.

一.note: 一 means one. Its dictionary tone is yī. In 一個 it is pronounced yí because 個 (gè) has a fourth tone.
一.memory: One horizontal stroke, drawn from left to right.

parts.label: 一
parts.name: one horizontal stroke
parts.description: 一 is a basic character in its own right. A single horizontal stroke writes the number one.

個.note: When counting people, put 個 between the number and the noun: 一個人 = one person. 個 is often pronounced lightly as ge in a phrase.
個.memory: A person component beside a box with another shape inside. Keep the right side roomy.

parts.label: 亻
parts.name: person
parts.description: Recognize the person component again. 個 is used to count people and many other things, so its use is wider than just people.

parts.label: 固
parts.name: 固 · gù
parts.description: 固 is a historical phonetic component. Its modern sound gù is only a rough clue to gè. The outer enclosure surrounds 古; close the outer bottom last.

人.note: 人 can mean person or people. Chinese nouns usually do not change shape for singular or plural; the number or context makes it clear.
人.memory: Two spreading strokes. Start the left-falling stroke first, then the right-falling stroke.

parts.label: 人
parts.name: person
parts.description: 人 is the full character person. Its narrow side form is 亻, which you have already seen in 你, 他, 們, and 個.

有.note: 有 means have. Put a person before it to say who has something. Without that subject, 有 + a noun phrase can introduce something that exists: there is or there are.
有.memory: Two strokes above a four-stroke lower block. These visual groups help you remember the shape.

parts.label: upper
parts.name: upper two strokes
parts.description: Start with the horizontal and the left-falling stroke. Treat them as a visual group rather than inventing a meaning for them.

parts.label: 月
parts.name: 月-shaped lower part
parts.description: This lower group resembles 月. A visible moon shape does not by itself explain the modern word have.

沒.note: Learn 沒 in 沒有 (méiyǒu): do not have, or there is not. 有 is negated with 沒, not 不.
沒.memory: Three water strokes on the left, then the four-stroke right side. Follow the Taiwan form shown in the guide.

parts.label: 氵
parts.name: water
parts.description: 氵 is a side form of 水 (water). It reflects other historical uses of 沒; it does not give the meaning of modern 沒有.

parts.label: 𠬛
parts.name: four-stroke right side
parts.description: Learn the upper turn and the lower 又-shaped strokes from the guide. This visible group is not a modern meaning equation for negation.

u2-pronouns.title: Change the person, keep the pattern
u2-pronouns.explanation: 他 means he or him; 她 means she or her. Both sound tā. Written Mandarin distinguishes them, while speech relies on context. 是 stays the same for every person: no separate forms for am, is, and are.
u2-pronouns.remember: Use 是 for an identity such as student. Chinese does not need a word for the English article a in this sentence.

u2-plurals.title: From I to we
u2-plurals.explanation: 我們 means we or us, 你們 means you when addressing more than one person, and 他們 means they or them. 們 has a light neutral tone. 他們 can refer to a male or mixed group.
u2-plurals.remember: 學生 stays the same for student and students. 們 is not a general plural ending for every noun, and you do not add it after a number + measure word.

u2-also.title: A small word for also
u2-also.explanation: 也 means also or too. It goes before the verb in these sentences, after the person. Use it when adding someone to something already said: you are a student; I am a student too.
u2-also.remember: Keep 也 before 是. Unlike English too, it does not go at the end of these sentences.

u2-not.title: Say that something is not true
u2-not.explanation: 不 goes before 是 to make it negative. 我不是學生 means I am not a student. If you also need 也, it comes before 不: 也不是 means is not either. The verb does not change, and there is no extra word for do or does.

examples.meaning: She is not a student either.

u2-not.remember: 不 is bù alone, but sounds bú before a fourth tone, as in 不是 (bú shì). To answer 你是學生嗎？, use 是 (yes, I am) or 不是 (no, I am not).

u2-possession.title: My, your, his, her
u2-possession.explanation: 的 links the person to the noun that follows. 我的學生 means my student; 你的學生 means your student. 他的 and 她的 mean his and her. The noun comes last, just as it does in the English phrase my student.
u2-possession.remember: 的 is light-toned de here. It can describe a relationship, such as a teacher and student, not just ownership. To make a full identity sentence, add the person + 是 before this noun phrase.

u2-counting.title: Count one person
u2-counting.explanation: 一 means one; 人 means person or people. When counting people in everyday speech, put 個 between the number and the noun: 一個人. 個 is a measure word (also called a classifier). It is common with people and many things, but other nouns need other measure words, which we will introduce when needed.
u2-counting.remember: 一 is yī alone. Before the fourth-tone word 個 (gè), it becomes yí. 個 often sounds light: yí ge. Do not add 們 to a counted noun. 我是學生 still works without 一個 when simply giving an identity.

u2-have.title: Have, or there is
u2-have.pattern: person + 有 + noun phrase / 有 + noun phrase
u2-have.explanation: 有 means have when a person comes before it. Imagine a tutor talking about a student: 她有一個學生 = she has one student. With no possessor before 有, it can mean there is or there are. 有 is already the verb; do not add 是 before it.
u2-have.remember: 一個學生 and 一個人 are the number + measure word + noun pattern you just learned.

u2-no-have.title: The special negative of 有
u2-no-have.pattern: person + 沒有 + noun / 沒有 + noun
u2-no-have.explanation: Use 沒有 to say do not have or there is not / there are no. 有 takes 沒 instead of 不: say 沒有, never 不有. Without a number, a Chinese noun can be singular or plural; context supplies that information.

examples.meaning: I do not have any students.

u2-no-have.remember: Keep the useful pair together: 有 ↔ 沒有. With 是, the negative is still 不是.

u2-have-question.title: Ask about having something
u2-have-question.explanation: The question rule from Unit 1 still works: add 嗎 to a statement. Keep the normal word order. To answer briefly, repeat the verb 有 for yes, or its negative 沒有 for no.

examples.meaning: Yes, I do. / No, I do not.

u2-have-question.remember: Answer this 有 question with 有 or 沒有. Use 是 or 不是 when answering an identity question with 是.

u2-he.note: 他 + 是 + 學生. The identity pattern stays the same when the person changes.

u2-she.note: 她 is the written pronoun she. It sounds the same as 他 (he).

u2-we.note: 我們 means we. 是 and 學生 do not change to agree with a plural subject.

u2-they-too.note: 他們 = they. 也 goes after the subject and before 是.

u2-not-student.note: 不 goes immediately before 是. Its spoken tone changes to bú before shì.

u2-neither.meaning: She is not a student either.
u2-neither.note: With also + not, keep the order 也 + 不 + 是.

u2-my-student.note: 我 + 的 makes my; 學生 is the noun. This is a noun phrase, not a full sentence.

u2-your-student.note: Put 的 between 你 and the noun 學生.

u2-she-my-student.note: 她 + 是 + 我的學生. The whole phrase my student takes the identity slot after 是.

u2-one-person.note: 一 (one) + 個 (measure word) + 人 (person). Here the phrase counts people; in other contexts it can also suggest being alone.

u2-one-student.note: Use the same measure word 個 with 學生. Do not add a plural ending to a counted noun.

u2-has-student.note: Imagine a tutor: 她 (she) + 有 (has) + 一個學生 (one student). 有 is the verb; no 是 is needed.

u2-there-is.note: With no possessor before 有, 有 introduces something that exists. 一個人 still uses the counting pattern.

u2-no-students.meaning: I do not have any students.
u2-no-students.note: Use 沒有, not 不有. 學生 needs no plural ending; here the negative makes the English meaning not any students natural.

u2-nobody.note: 沒有 + 人 = there is no person / nobody. No subject is needed in this existence pattern.

u2-have-question.note: Add 嗎 to 你有學生. A short answer is 有 (yes) or 沒有 (no).

u2-they-my-students.pinyin: tāmen yě shì wǒ de xuéshēng
u2-they-my-students.note: 他們 (they) + 也 (also) + 是 (are) + 我的學生 (my students). 學生 remains unchanged in the plural.
